q.q: The two-kingdom system of classification (Plantae and Animalia) was proposed by:
q.e: Carolus Linnaeus proposed the two-kingdom system, classifying all living organisms into Plantae and Animalia.

q.q: Which criterion was NOT used by R.H. Whittaker while proposing the Five Kingdom Classification?
q.e: Whittaker's five kingdom system was based on cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships — not habitat.

q.q: Which of these organisms was placed in a separate kingdom, Protista, mainly because it did not fit into the plant-animal division?
q.e: Unicellular eukaryotes like Amoeba could not be clearly classified as plants or animals, leading to the creation of Kingdom Protista.

q.q: A group of organisms sharing common features and morphology which can interbreed and produce fertile offspring is called:
q.e: A species is a group of individuals with common features that are capable of interbreeding to produce fertile offspring.

q.q: Systematics is the branch of science dealing with:
o: Classification and diversity of organisms along with their relationships
q.e: Systematics deals with the diversification of living organisms and their relationships, and also classification based on these relationships.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Species is the basic unit; a group of related species forms a genus; a group of related genera forms a family.

q.q: The Five Kingdom system of classification was proposed in the year:
q.e: R.H. Whittaker proposed the Five Kingdom classification in 1969.

q.q: Which kingdom in the Five Kingdom system includes only prokaryotic organisms?
q.e: Kingdom Monera includes only prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria, which lack a well-defined nucleus.

q.q: Which statement correctly describes the criteria used in the Five Kingdom Classification?
o: Only mode of nutrition was considered
Cell structure, body organisation, nutrition, reproduction and phylogeny were all considered
q.e: Whittaker used multiple criteria together — cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships.

q.q: Fungi were placed in a separate kingdom mainly due to their:
o: Saprophytic/heterotrophic mode of nutrition and cell wall of chitin
q.e: Fungi have a heterotrophic (mostly saprophytic) mode of nutrition and a chitinous cell wall, distinguishing them from plants.

q.q: Which of the following kingdoms consists exclusively of multicellular, eukaryotic, autotrophic organisms?
q.e: Kingdom Plantae consists of multicellular, eukaryotic, photosynthetic (autotrophic) organisms.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Monera = prokaryotes; Protista = unicellular eukaryotes; Fungi = heterotrophic organisms with a chitinous cell wall.

q.q: Bacteria having a rod shape are called:
q.e: Rod-shaped bacteria are called bacillus; spherical are coccus, comma-shaped are vibrio, and spiral are spirillum.

q.q: Archaebacteria differ from other bacteria mainly due to differences in their:
q.e: Archaebacteria have a distinct cell wall composition, which allows them to survive in extreme environments like hot springs and salty areas.

q.q: Which of the following correctly describes Mycoplasma?
o: Bacteria with a rigid cell wall
Organisms completely lacking a cell wall
q.e: Mycoplasma are unique among prokaryotes as they completely lack a cell wall, and are the smallest known living cells.

q.q: Heterocysts, the site of nitrogen fixation in cyanobacteria, are found in organisms such as:
q.e: Nostoc and Anabaena are cyanobacteria possessing specialised, thick-walled cells called heterocysts, which fix atmospheric nitrogen.

q.q: Bacteria that obtain nutrition through photosynthesis using bacteriochlorophyll are called:
q.e: Photosynthetic autotrophic bacteria contain bacteriochlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis in an anaerobic manner.

q.q: Arrange the following bacterial shapes with their correct names: spherical, comma-shaped, spiral, rod-shaped correspond respectively to:
q.e: Spherical = Coccus, comma-shaped = Vibrio, spiral = Spirillum, rod-shaped = Bacillus.

q.q: Diatoms belong to which group of protists?
q.e: Diatoms are chrysophytes with cell walls embedded with silica, forming indestructible "diatomaceous earth".

q.q: The organism that possesses characteristics of both plants and animals, having chlorophyll but also a gullet, is:
q.e: Euglena has chlorophyll (autotrophic in sunlight) but behaves heterotrophically in the absence of light, using a gullet-like structure.

q.q: Which statement about slime moulds is correct?
o: They have a rigid cell wall of cellulose
They form an aggregation called a plasmodium under favourable conditions
q.e: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists that form an aggregation called a plasmodium under favourable conditions.

q.q: Dinoflagellates that cause the phenomenon of 'red tide' in the sea are mostly:
q.e: Red dinoflagellates, when they multiply rapidly, may make the sea appear red, a phenomenon called 'red tide'.

q.q: Amoeba, Paramecium and Plasmodium are grouped under which protist group?
q.e: Protozoans are heterotrophic protists including Amoeba, Paramecium, and the parasitic Plasmodium.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Chrysophytes include diatoms; dinoflagellates have two flagella; protozoans are heterotrophic like Amoeba.

q.q: The vegetative body of a fungus is made up of long, slender thread-like structures called:
q.e: The fungal body consists of thread-like hyphae, and a network of hyphae is called a mycelium.

q.q: Sexual spores found in Ascomycetes (sac fungi) are called:
q.e: Ascomycetes produce endogenously formed sexual spores called ascospores, contained within a sac-like ascus.

q.q: Which statement correctly describes Deuteromycetes (Fungi Imperfecti)?
o: They are the only fungi with septate hyphae
Only asexual/vegetative phases are known; classified purely on the basis of morphology
q.e: Deuteromycetes are called Fungi Imperfecti because only their asexual or vegetative phases are known, and they are classified purely on morphology.

q.q: In the fungal sexual cycle, the fusion of two haploid nuclei to form a diploid zygote nucleus is termed:
q.e: Karyogamy is the fusion of two haploid nuclei following plasmogamy, forming a diploid zygote nucleus.

q.q: Yeast, used in baking and brewing, belongs to which class of fungi?
q.e: Yeast (Saccharomyces) is an Ascomycete widely used in baking and brewing industries.

q.q: Arrange the three main steps of the fungal sexual cycle in correct order:
q.e: The fungal sexual cycle proceeds: Plasmogamy (fusion of protoplasms) → Karyogamy (fusion of nuclei) → Meiosis (formation of haploid spores).

q.q: Plants are called autotrophs mainly because they:
o: Depend on other organisms for food
Synthesize their own food using chlorophyll and sunlight
q.e: Plants are autotrophs as they can synthesise their own food through photosynthesis using chlorophyll.

q.q: Insectivorous plants like Nepenthes and Drosera are considered partially heterotrophic because they:
o: Trap and digest insects to supplement nutrition
q.e: Insectivorous plants photosynthesise but also trap and digest insects, supplementing nutrition, especially nitrogen.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes plant cells from animal cells?
o: Animal cells have chloroplasts, plant cells do not
Plant cells lack a cell wall, unlike animal cells
Plant cells have an eukaryotic cellulosic cell wall which animal cells lack
q.e: Plant cells possess a eukaryotic cell wall made of cellulose, a feature typically absent in animal cells.

q.q: Cuscuta, a parasitic plant, is an example of:
o: A plant lacking chlorophyll that derives nutrition from a host
q.e: Cuscuta is a parasitic, non-chlorophyllous plant that derives its nutrition directly from a host plant.

q.q: Animals are heterotrophic because they:
o: Depend directly or indirectly on plants for food
q.e: Animals cannot synthesise their own food and depend directly or indirectly on plants, making them heterotrophic.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Dionaea (Venus flytrap) and Drosera (sundew) are insectivorous; Cuscuta is a parasitic, non-green plant.

q.q: Viruses are described as obligate parasites because they:
o: Can multiply only inside a living host cell
q.e: Viruses lack their own metabolic machinery and can replicate only inside a living host cell, making them obligate parasites.

q.q: The protein coat surrounding the genetic material of a virus is called:
q.e: The capsid is the protein coat made of small subunits called capsomeres that encloses the viral genetic material.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes viroids from viruses?
o: Viroids are free RNA without a protein coat, unlike viruses which have a capsid
Viroids have a higher molecular weight than viruses
Viroids have a protein coat, viruses do not
q.e: Viroids consist only of free RNA without a protein coat and have a much lower molecular weight than viruses, which possess a capsid.

q.q: Prions, associated with diseases like Mad Cow Disease, are best described as:
o: Infectious protein particles lacking any nucleic acid
q.e: Prions are abnormally folded infectious proteins that lack nucleic acid, causing neurological diseases such as BSE (Mad Cow Disease).

q.q: T.O. Diener discovered which infectious agent smaller than viruses?
q.e: T.O. Diener discovered viroids, infectious agents even smaller than viruses, consisting of free RNA.

q.q: Arrange in order of increasing structural complexity: Viroid, Virus, Prion (in terms of possessing both nucleic acid and protein coat):
q.e: Prion has neither nucleic acid nor a coat (protein only); Viroid has RNA but no coat; Virus has both nucleic acid and a protein coat.

q.q: A lichen is a symbiotic association between:
q.e: A lichen is a symbiotic association between an alga (phycobiont) and a fungus (mycobiont).

q.q: In a lichen association, the alga (phycobiont) is responsible for:
o: Absorbing water and minerals, providing shelter
q.e: The phycobiont (algal partner) is autotrophic and photosynthetic, preparing food for the lichen association.

q.q: Which statement explains why lichens are considered good indicators of air pollution?
o: They grow only in polluted areas
They absorb pollutants and grow larger
They are highly sensitive to sulphur dioxide/pollutants and do not grow in polluted areas
They thrive equally in all environments
q.e: Lichens are highly sensitive to pollutants like sulphur dioxide and do not grow in polluted areas, making them good pollution indicators.

q.q: In a lichen, the fungal partner (mycobiont) primarily provides:
o: Shelter and absorbs water and mineral nutrients for the alga
q.e: The mycobiont (fungal partner) is heterotrophic; it provides shelter and absorbs water and mineral nutrients for the association.

q.q: Lichens play an important ecological role as pioneers in:
q.e: Lichens are often pioneer organisms in plant succession, colonising bare rocks before other plants can grow.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Phycobiont (algal partner) is autotrophic and prepares food; mycobiont (fungal partner) is heterotrophic and provides shelter.

q.q: Aristotle's habitat-based grouping of animals divided them into:
q.e: Besides the Enaima/Anaima division by blood colour, Aristotle also grouped animals by habitat into Aquatic and Terrestrial forms.

q.q: Linnaeus's Two Kingdom system placed fungi under the kingdom:
q.e: In the two-kingdom system, all non-green, non-motile organisms including fungi were grouped under Plantae, since the system used only two kingdoms.

q.q: In the Five Kingdom Classification, which characteristic was used to separate Monera from all other kingdoms?
q.e: Monera is the only kingdom of prokaryotes; all other four kingdoms (Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) consist of eukaryotic organisms.

q.q: Cyanobacteria are also commonly known as:
q.e: Cyanobacteria (e.g., Nostoc, Anabaena) are photosynthetic prokaryotes commonly called blue-green algae.

q.q: Which statement about archaebacteria is correct?
o: They have the same cell wall composition as other bacteria
They can survive in extreme habitats like hot springs, salty areas and marshy areas
q.e: Archaebacteria have a distinct cell wall that allows them to survive in extreme environments — halophiles in salty areas, thermoacidophiles in hot springs, and methanogens in marshy areas.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Amoeboid protozoans (Entamoeba) move via pseudopodia; flagellated protozoans (Trypanosoma) have flagella; ciliated protozoans (Paramecium) have cilia; sporozoans (Plasmodium) have an infectious spore-like stage.

q.q: The fungal class characterised by the presence of coenocytic (aseptate) mycelium is:
q.e: Phycomycetes (e.g., Mucor, Rhizopus) have aseptate, coenocytic mycelium.

q.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Plantae from Animalia?
o: Animalia has cellulose cell walls, Plantae does not
Plantae shows unlimited (indeterminate) growth via meristems, Animalia shows determinate growth
Plantae lacks any mode of reproduction
q.e: Plants exhibit indeterminate growth throughout life due to the presence of meristems, whereas animals show determinate growth, attaining a fixed body size at maturity.

q.q: Movement of materials within the plant body occurs through vascular tissues, whereas in animals it occurs mainly through the:
q.e: Animals possess a circulatory system (blood/lymph) for internal transport, unlike plants which use vascular tissues (xylem and phloem).

q.q: The scientist who first crystallised the Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) and showed it to be largely protein was:
q.e: W.M. Stanley (1935) showed that viruses could be crystallised and that the crystals consist largely of protein.

q.q: Match Column A with Column B and choose the correct combination:
q.e: TMV is a rod-shaped plant virus with a single-stranded RNA genome; Bacteriophage T4 has a double-stranded DNA genome and infects bacteria; HIV is a retrovirus with an RNA genome that uses reverse transcriptase.

q.q: In the association forming a lichen, the fungal component (mycobiont) belongs mainly to:
q.e: The mycobiont in lichens is generally a member of Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes.

q.q: The Artificial System of classification was proposed by:
q.e: The Artificial System, based on superficial vegetative and androecium characters, was given by Linnaeus.

q.q: Bentham and Hooker proposed the:
q.e: George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker proposed the Natural System of classification.

q.q: Cytotaxonomy uses which of the following as its basis?
q.e: Cytotaxonomy is based on cytological information such as chromosome number, structure and behaviour.

q.q: Chemotaxonomy classifies plants based on their:
q.e: Chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of a plant to resolve taxonomic doubts.

q.q: Algae are generally:
q.e: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, thalloid and autotrophic organisms.

q.q: Vegetative reproduction in algae mainly occurs by:
q.e: Vegetative reproduction in algae occurs by fragmentation, with each fragment growing into a new thallus.

q.q: Fusion of two similar-sized motile gametes is called:
q.e: Isogamy is the fusion of two gametes similar in size and motility, as in Chlamydomonas.

q.q: Agar is commercially obtained from:
q.e: Agar, used to culture microbes, is obtained from the red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria.

q.q: Chlorophyceae members are commonly called:
q.e: Chlorophyceae members are called green algae due to the dominance of chlorophyll a and b.

q.q: The stored food in Phaeophyceae is:
q.e: Phaeophyceae store food as complex carbohydrates such as laminarin or mannitol.

q.q: The pigment r-phycoerythrin is characteristic of:
q.e: r-Phycoerythrin is the red pigment characteristic of Rhodophyceae (red algae).

q.q: Which of these is an example of Phaeophyceae?
q.e: Ectocarpus is a well-known example of Phaeophyceae (brown algae).

q.q: Bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because they:
q.e: Bryophytes live on land but require water for the antherozoids to swim to the archegonium and fertilize the egg.

q.q: The dominant phase in the life cycle of a bryophyte is the:
q.e: In bryophytes, the haploid gametophyte is the dominant, independent phase.

q.q: The male sex organ in bryophytes is called the:
q.e: The antheridium is the male sex organ in bryophytes, producing biflagellate antherozoids.

q.q: Peat, used as fuel, is obtained from:
q.e: Sphagnum, a moss, yields peat which is used as a fuel.

q.q: Marchantia belongs to the class:
q.e: Marchantia is a well-known example of the Liverworts class of Bryophyta.

q.q: Gemmae are found in specialized structures called:
q.e: Gemmae are green, multicellular asexual buds produced in gemma cups on the thallus of liverworts.

q.q: The creeping, filamentous first stage of the moss gametophyte is called the:
q.e: The protonema is the creeping, green, filamentous stage that develops directly from a germinating moss spore.

q.q: Funaria is a well-known example of:
q.e: Funaria is a common example of the moss class of Bryophyta.

q.q: Pteridophytes were the first plants to possess:
q.e: Pteridophytes were the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissue (xylem and phloem).

q.q: The dominant phase in pteridophytes is the:
q.e: The dominant phase in pteridophytes is the diploid sporophyte.

q.q: Selaginella and Salvinia are examples of pteridophytes that are:
q.e: Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous, producing both microspores and megaspores.

q.q: The free-living photosynthetic gametophyte of a fern is called the:
q.e: The prothallus is the small, free-living, photosynthetic gametophyte of pteridophytes.

q.q: Gymnosperm seeds are described as naked because:
o: They are not enclosed by an ovary wall
q.e: In gymnosperms, ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall, so the seeds formed remain naked.

q.q: Coralloid roots, associated with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, are found in:
q.e: Coralloid roots showing symbiotic association with N2-fixing cyanobacteria are found in Cycas.

q.q: Mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association of fungi with the roots of:
q.e: Mycorrhiza is the symbiotic association of fungi with the roots of Pinus.

q.q: Which of the following is called a 'living fossil'?
q.e: Ginkgo is commonly referred to as a living fossil among gymnosperms.

q.q: In angiosperms, the seeds are enclosed within the:
q.e: In angiosperms, following fertilization, seeds develop enclosed within a fruit.

q.q: Angiosperms are divided into two classes, namely:
q.e: Angiosperms are classified into two classes: the Dicotyledons and the Monocotyledons.

q.q: The smallest known flowering plant is:
q.e: Wolffia is the smallest known flowering plant.

q.q: Pollen grains and ovules in angiosperms develop within:
q.e: In angiosperms, pollen grains and ovules develop within specialized reproductive structures called flowers.

q.q: Match Column I (System) with Column II (Basis) and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Artificial System = vegetative+androecium; Natural System = morphology/anatomy/embryology; Phylogenetic = evolutionary relationships; Cytotaxonomy = chromosome number.

q.q: Match Column I (Algal Class) with Column II (Pigments) and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Chlorophyceae has chlorophyll a,b; Phaeophyceae has chlorophyll a,c + fucoxanthin; Rhodophyceae has chlorophyll a,d + r-phycoerythrin.

q.q: Match Column I (Algal Class) with Column II (Stored Food) and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Chlorophyceae stores starch in pyrenoids; Phaeophyceae stores laminarin/mannitol; Rhodophyceae stores Floridean starch.

q.q: Match Column I (Bryophyte group) with Column II (Example) and choose the correct combination:
o: Both A and B match ii
Both A and B match i
q.e: Marchantia is a liverwort; Funaria is a moss.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Description) and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Antheridium is the male sex organ, archegonium is the female sex organ, and the prothallus is the free-living gametophyte.

q.q: Match Column I (Gymnosperm Class) with Column II (Example) and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Cycadopsida includes Cycas; Coniferopsida includes Pinus; Gnetopsida includes Gnetum.

q.q: Match Column I (Root association) with Column II (Plant) and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Mycorrhiza is a fungal association found in Pinus roots; coralloid roots (with N2-fixing cyanobacteria) are found in Cycas.

q.q: Match Column I (Reproduction type) with Column II (Example) and choose the correct combination:
q.e: Isogamous fusion occurs in Spirogyra; anisogamous fusion in some Chlamydomonas species; oogamous fusion in Volvox and Fucus.

q.q:
Statement I: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are classified under Algae in the current five-kingdom system.
Statement II: Cyanobacteria are prokaryotic and lack a well-defined nucleus.
Choose the correct option:
o: Both I and II are true, and II explains I
Both I and II are true, but II does not explain I
I is false, II is true
I is true, II is false
q.e: Cyanobacteria have now been excluded from Algae (they are prokaryotic Monera), so Statement I is false while Statement II is true.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about bryophytes is/are correct?
(i) They are dominant in the gametophytic phase
(ii) Water is required for fertilization
(iii) The sporophyte is completely independent of the gametophyte
q.e: Statement (iii) is incorrect — the sporophyte in bryophytes remains attached to and dependent on the gametophyte for nutrition.

q.q:
Consider the following statements about Pteridophytes:
(i) They possess vascular tissue
(ii) The dominant phase is the gametophyte
(iii) Genera like Selaginella are heterosporous
Which of these are correct?
q.e: Statement (ii) is incorrect — the sporophyte, not the gametophyte, is the dominant phase in pteridophytes.

q.q:
Statement I: In gymnosperms, the ovules are enclosed within an ovary wall.
Statement II: Seeds in gymnosperms remain naked even after fertilization.
Choose the correct option:
o: I is true, II is false
I is false, II is true
I is true, II is true
q.e: Gymnosperm ovules are NOT enclosed by an ovary wall (Statement I is false), so the resulting seeds remain naked (Statement II is true).

q.q:
Which combination of statements about algae is correct?
(i) Vegetative reproduction occurs by fragmentation
(ii) Zoospores are non-motile structures
(iii) Sexual reproduction can be isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous
q.e: Statement (ii) is incorrect — zoospores are flagellated and motile, not non-motile.

q.q:
Statement I: Chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of a plant to resolve taxonomic doubts.
Statement II: Chemotaxonomy has entirely replaced the need for morphological classification.
Choose the correct option:
q.e: Chemotaxonomy is a supporting tool used alongside morphological classification, not a replacement for it.

q.q:
Consider the following statements:
(i) Liverworts have a thalloid body
(ii) Mosses are attached to the soil by unicellular rhizoids
(iii) Sphagnum (a moss) yields peat
Which of these are correct?
q.e: Statement (ii) is incorrect — mosses have multicellular, branched rhizoids; unicellular rhizoids are characteristic of liverworts.

q.q:
Statement I: The pollen grain in gymnosperms represents a reduced male gametophyte.
Statement II: Male and female gametophytes in gymnosperms have an independent existence outside the sporangia.
Choose the correct option:
q.e: Male and female gametophytes in gymnosperms do NOT have independent existence — they remain within the sporangia.

q.q: Angiosperms are also called flowering plants because their seeds develop inside:
o: An ovary that matures into a fruit
q.e: In angiosperms, ovules are enclosed within an ovary, which develops into a fruit after fertilisation, hence they are also called flowering plants with covered (angio-) seeds.

q.q: Based on the number of cotyledons present in the seed, angiosperms are classified into:
q.e: Angiosperms are divided into two classes, monocotyledons (one cotyledon) and dicotyledons (two cotyledons), based on the number of cotyledons in their seeds.

q.q: The vegetative growth in algae occurs mainly by:
q.e: Vegetative growth in algae occurs through cell division, and fragmentation is a common asexual reproductive method in filamentous forms.

q.q: In bryophytes, the dominant, photosynthetic phase of the life cycle is the:
q.e: In bryophytes, the gametophyte is the dominant, free-living, photosynthetic phase, while the sporophyte remains attached to and dependent on it.

q.q: Which statement correctly describes heterospory in pteridophytes?
o: All pteridophytes produce only one kind of spore
Heterosporous pteridophytes (e.g., Selaginella, Salvinia) produce microspores and megaspores
Heterospory means spores of different colours
q.e: Some pteridophytes like Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous, producing two kinds of spores — microspores and megaspores — and this heterosporous condition is significant as it is the precursor to seed habit.

q.q: The common name for members of Rhodophyceae, which are typically found in marine habitats at greater depths, is:
q.e: Rhodophyceae members, called red algae, owe their colour to the red pigment r-phycoerythrin and are commonly found in marine habitats, often at considerable depths.

q.q: Which criterion separates animals with cellular level of organisation from those with tissue level of organisation?
q.e: Level of organisation is a fundamental basis of animal classification.

q.q: Match the basis of classification with its description.
q.e: Symmetry concerns body halves, coelom is the body cavity, and notochord is an axial supporting rod.

q.q: Choose the correct statement.
o: External appearance alone is the most reliable basis of animal classification.
Levels of organisation, symmetry and nature of coelom are useful classification criteria.
All animals have the same type of circulatory system.
Presence of chlorophyll is a basis of animal classification.
q.e: Animal classification uses structural and developmental features such as organisation, symmetry and coelom.

q.q: An animal that can be divided into equal halves by any plane passing through its central axis shows:
q.e: Radially symmetrical animals can be divided into similar halves by any plane through the central axis.

q.q: Match the animal group with its body-plan condition.
q.e: Sponges are generally asymmetrical, cnidarians radial, and annelids bilateral.

q.q: A transverse diagram shows a body cavity completely lined by mesoderm on both the body-wall and gut sides. The animal is:
q.e: A true coelom is completely lined by mesoderm.

q.q: Repeated serial arrangement of similar body units along the longitudinal axis is called:
q.e: Metamerism is true segmentation into repeated serial units.

q.q: Match the feature with the appropriate group.
q.e: Annelids are metamerically segmented, chordates possess a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and non-chordates generally have a ventral solid nerve cord.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes chordates from non-chordates?
o: Chordates have a ventral, solid nerve cord.
Chordates possess a notochord at least at some stage of life.
All non-chordates possess pharyngeal gill slits.
q.e: A notochord is a defining chordate character, present at least during embryonic development.

q.q: The water current in a sponge finally leaves the body through the:
q.e: Water enters through ostia, reaches the spongocoel/canal system and exits through the osculum.

q.q: Match the sponge cell/structure with its function.
q.e: Choanocytes drive water currents, spicules form the skeleton and amoebocytes transport food.

q.q: The stinging capsules characteristic of cnidarians are called:
q.e: Cnidoblasts contain nematocysts used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey.

q.q: Match the cnidarian with its common form or feature.
q.e: Hydra is a polyp, Aurelia is a medusa and Obelia displays metagenesis.

q.q: Which statement is correct for Coelenterata (Cnidaria)?
o: They have an incomplete digestive system with a single opening.
q.e: Cnidarians are diploblastic and have a gastrovascular cavity with one opening.

q.q: Locomotion in ctenophores is brought about by:
q.e: Eight rows of ciliary comb plates bring about locomotion in ctenophores.

q.q: Match the feature with the correct phylum.
q.e: Ctenophores have colloblasts, cnidarians cnidoblasts and sponges choanocytes.

q.q: The excretory structures of flatworms are:
q.e: Flame cells or protonephridia perform osmoregulation and excretion in platyhelminths.

q.q: Match the flatworm with its usual mode of life.
q.e: Planaria is free-living, Taenia is an intestinal endoparasite and Fasciola is a liver parasite.

q.q: Select the correct combination for Platyhelminthes.
q.e: Flatworms are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and acoelomate.

q.q: Aschelminthes are commonly called:
q.e: Aschelminthes are cylindrical, unsegmented roundworms.

q.q: Match the roundworm with its association.
q.e: Ascaris is an intestinal parasite, Wuchereria causes filariasis and Ancylostoma is hookworm.

q.q: Which statement about aschelminths is correct?
o: They possess a pseudocoel and usually have separate sexes.
They have nephridia and closed circulation.
q.e: Aschelminths are pseudocoelomates and generally dioecious.

q.q: Excretion in earthworm is carried out by:
q.e: Nephridia are the excretory organs of annelids such as earthworm.

q.q: Match the annelid with its characteristic structure or habitat.
q.e: Nereis has parapodia, earthworm has setae and leech lacks setae.

q.q: A worm diagram has repeated ring-like units marked from anterior to posterior. This feature indicates:
q.e: Repeated serial segments are a hallmark of annelids.

q.q: The body appendages of arthropods are characteristically:
q.e: Jointed appendages are the most characteristic feature of Arthropoda.

q.q: Match the arthropod with its excretory organ.
q.e: Insects use Malpighian tubules, crustaceans green glands and arachnids commonly use Malpighian tubules/coxal glands; the standard NCERT pairing is Prawn–green glands.

q.q: Which statement is correct for Arthropoda?
o: They have a closed circulatory system and nephridia.
Their body is covered by a chitinous exoskeleton.
They are all aquatic and breathe by gills.
q.e: Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton and an open circulatory system.

q.q: The rasping feeding organ found in most molluscs is the:
q.e: The radula is a rasping feeding organ; it is absent in bivalves.

q.q: Match the mollusc with its diagnostic feature.
q.e: Pila has a shell and foot, Unio is bivalved, and Octopus has arms with suckers.

q.q: The water vascular system of echinoderms principally helps in:
q.e: Tube feet of the water vascular system function in locomotion, feeding and respiration.

q.q: Match the echinoderm with its common name.
q.e: Asterias is starfish, Echinus sea urchin and Antedon sea lily.

q.q: Which statement about Echinodermata is correct?
o: Adults are bilateral and larvae radial.
They are freshwater animals with a pseudocoel.
Adults are radially symmetrical, while larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
Their body has a chitinous exoskeleton with jointed legs.
q.e: Echinoderm adults are radially symmetrical; their larvae show bilateral symmetry.

q.q: The body of Balanoglossus is divided into:
q.e: Hemichordates have a characteristic proboscis, collar and trunk.

q.q: Match the feature with Hemichordata.
q.e: Hemichordates are marine, excrete through a proboscis gland and include Balanoglossus.

q.q: Why are hemichordates placed in a separate phylum rather than in Chordata?
o: They have no organ-system level of organisation.
q.e: Hemichordates have pharyngeal gill slits but do not possess a true notochord.

q.q: Which is NOT a characteristic chordate feature?
q.e: Chordates have a dorsal hollow nerve cord, unlike the usual ventral solid cord of non-chordates.

q.q: Match the chordate subphylum with its example.
q.e: Urochordata includes Herdmania, Cephalochordata includes Branchiostoma and Vertebrata includes humans.

q.q: Cyclostomes possess a:
q.e: Cyclostomes are jawless vertebrates with a circular sucking mouth.

q.q: Match the class feature with Cyclostomata.
q.e: Cyclostomes include Petromyzon and Myxine, lack paired fins and migrate to freshwater for spawning.

q.q: Which statement is correct about cyclostomes?
o: They are exclusively freshwater throughout life.
They are ectoparasites on other fishes and have six to fifteen pairs of gill slits.
They have placoid scales and a heterocercal tail.
They possess an operculum covering four pairs of gills.
q.e: Cyclostomes are ectoparasitic; they have 6–15 pairs of gill slits and no paired fins.

q.q: The scales of cartilaginous fishes are:
q.e: Chondrichthyans such as sharks possess placoid scales.

q.q: Match the cartilaginous fish with its special feature.
q.e: Torpedo has electric organs, Trygon has a sting and Scoliodon is the dogfish.

q.q: A fish diagram shows five exposed gill slits with no operculum and a heterocercal tail. It represents:
q.e: Exposed gill slits, placoid scales and a heterocercal tail are features of Chondrichthyes.

q.q: The bony flap covering the gills of most Osteichthyes is the:
q.e: In bony fishes, four pairs of gills are covered by an operculum.

q.q: Match the bony fish with its identifying feature.
q.e: Hippocampus is seahorse, Exocoetus flying fish and Labeo (Rohu) a freshwater bony fish.

q.q: Which feature correctly explains buoyancy in most bony fishes?
q.e: The air bladder helps most Osteichthyes maintain buoyancy.

q.q: Amphibians generally have a heart with:
q.e: Most amphibians have a three-chambered heart.

q.q: Match the amphibian with the correct description.
q.e: Salamandra is salamander, Bufo is toad and Rana is frog.

q.q: A vertebrate diagram shows moist scaleless skin and webbed digits. The specimen is most likely:
q.e: Moist, glandular, scaleless skin is characteristic of amphibians.

q.q: The skin of reptiles is characteristically:
o: Dry and cornified with epidermal scales/scutes
q.e: Reptilian skin is dry, cornified and generally bears epidermal scales or scutes.

q.q: Match the reptile with its distinctive group.
q.e: Chelone is a turtle, Crocodilus a crocodile and Naja a snake.

q.q: Select the correct statement about reptiles.
o: All reptiles have a three-chambered heart.
They have moist skin and external fertilisation.
q.e: Most reptiles have a three-chambered heart, but crocodiles have four chambers.

q.q: The body of birds is generally covered with:
q.e: Feathers are the diagnostic body covering of Aves.

q.q: Match the bird with its adaptation or example.
q.e: Penguin is flightless, kiwi is a flightless bird and ostrich is a large cursorial bird.

q.q: The structure that provides nourishment to young ones in female mammals is the:
q.e: Mammary glands are the defining feature of Mammalia.

q.q: Match the mammal with its reproductive category.
q.e: Ornithorhynchus is oviparous, kangaroo marsupial and humans placental mammals.

q.q: Which combination is diagnostic of Mammalia?
o: Hair, external ear pinnae and mammary glands
Placoid scales, gill slits and cartilage
q.e: Hair, mammary glands and usually external ear pinnae distinguish mammals.

q.q: Which phylum is the largest in Kingdom Animalia?
q.e: Arthropoda is the largest phylum of animals.

q.q: Match the group with its main excretory structure.
q.e: Platyhelminthes has flame cells, Annelida nephridia and Arthropoda Malpighian tubules.

q.q: Which sequence correctly represents increasing complexity of organisation in the listed groups?
q.e: Porifera has cellular level, Cnidaria tissue level, Platyhelminthes organ level and Annelida organ-system level of organisation.

q.q: The tap root system develops directly from the:
q.e: The radicle elongates directly to form the primary/tap root.

q.q: Root hairs develop in which region of the root?
q.e: Root hairs develop from the epidermis in the region of maturation.

q.q: Match Column I (Root type) with Column II (Example):
q.e: Mustard has a tap root, wheat a fibrous root, and banyan has prop roots.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about pneumatophores is/are correct?
(i) They grow vertically upward from the mud
(ii) They aid in gaseous exchange
(iii) They are found in mangrove plants
q.e: All three statements correctly describe pneumatophores in mangroves like Rhizophora.

q.q: The stem develops from which part of the embryo?
q.e: The stem arises directly from the plumule.

q.q: A potato tuber is classified as a modified stem because it:
q.e: Presence of nodes ('eyes') bearing axillary buds confirms the tuber is a stem, not a root.

q.q: Match Column I (Modified stem) with Column II (Example):
q.e: Rhizome-Ginger, Corm-Colocasia, Bulb-Onion.

q.q: Reticulate venation is characteristic of:
q.e: Dicot leaves typically show net-like, reticulate venation.

q.q: Neem shows which type of compound leaf?
q.e: Neem has leaflets arranged along a common rachis — pinnately compound.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about phyllotaxy is/are correct?
(i) Alternate phyllotaxy has one leaf per node
(ii) Opposite phyllotaxy has a pair of leaves per node
(iii) Whorled phyllotaxy has more than two leaves per node
q.e: All three statements correctly describe the three phyllotaxy types.

q.q: In racemose inflorescence, flowers are arranged:
q.e: Racemose inflorescences show acropetal succession — older flowers at the base.

q.q: In cymose inflorescence, the main axis:
q.e: The main axis ends in a terminal flower, limiting further growth.

q.q: Match Column I (Inflorescence type) with Column II (Growth pattern):
o: Both A and B match i
Both A and B match ii
q.e: Racemose = continuous growth; Cymose = limited growth ending in a flower.

q.q: Which whorls of the flower are reproductive?
q.e: Androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (carpels) are the reproductive whorls.

q.q: In hypogynous flowers, the ovary is:
q.e: The gynoecium sits highest on the thalamus, making the ovary superior.

q.q: Match Column I (Placentation) with Column II (Example):
q.e: Marginal-Pea, Axile-Tomato, Parietal-Mustard.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about aestivation is/are correct?
(i) Valvate aestivation shows margins that just touch
(ii) Vexillary aestivation is seen in the pea family
(iii) Imbricate aestivation shows margins overlapping unevenly
q.e: All three statements correctly describe these aestivation types.

q.q: A fruit that develops without fertilization is called:
q.e: Parthenocarpic fruits form without fertilization and lack seeds, e.g. banana.

q.q: Mango and coconut are examples of which fruit type?
q.e: Both develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are drupes.

q.q: The scutellum is found in:
q.e: Scutellum is the single shield-shaped cotyledon of monocot seeds like maize.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the pericarp is/are correct?
(i) It develops from the ovary wall
(ii) It may be dry or fleshy
(iii) When fleshy, it has three layers: epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp
q.e: All three statements are correct descriptions of the pericarp.

q.q: Solanaceae is commonly known as the:
q.e: Solanaceae is commonly called the potato family.

q.q: The gynoecium in Solanaceae is:
q.e: Solanaceae has a bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary.

q.q: Match Column I (Solanaceae plant) with Column II (Use):
q.e: Potato is food, Chilli is a spice, Ashwagandha is medicinal.

q.q: Velamen tissue, which helps in absorption of moisture from the air, is found in the roots of:
q.e: Epiphytes like orchids develop a special type of aerial root with a spongy tissue called velamen that absorbs moisture from the atmosphere.

q.q: Adventitious roots arise from parts of the plant other than the:
q.e: Roots that develop from any part of the plant body other than the radicle are called adventitious roots, e.g., in monocot plants like grass, wheat and banana.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the functions of roots is/are correct?
(i) Roots absorb water and minerals from the soil
(ii) Roots always perform photosynthesis
(iii) Some roots provide mechanical support to the plant
(iv) Roots never store reserve food
q.e: Roots primarily absorb water and minerals and anchor/support the plant; they normally lack chlorophyll and do not photosynthesise, and many roots (e.g., carrot, turnip) do store reserve food.

q.q: A root that is thick at the base and gradually tapers towards the tip, as seen in carrot, is called a:
q.e: A conical root is thick at the base and gradually tapers towards the apex, as seen in carrot; a napiform root (e.g., turnip) is instead swollen and disc-like.

q.q: The region of the stem that bears leaves, buds or branches is called the:
q.e: A node is the region of the stem where leaves, branches and buds arise; the portion between two successive nodes is called the internode.

q.q: Thorns, seen in plants like Citrus and Bougainvillea, are modified:
q.e: Thorns are hard, pointed structures that develop from axillary buds and help protect the plant from browsing animals.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about underground stem modifications is/are correct?
(i) They store food reserves
(ii) They help perennation (survival through unfavourable seasons)
(iii) Rhizome, tuber, bulb and corm are all examples
(iv) They always develop from the radicle
q.e: Underground stems such as rhizome, tuber, bulb and corm are modified for storage of food and perennation; they develop from the plumule of the embryo, not the radicle (roots develop from the radicle).

q.q: Tendrils that help a plant climb, as seen in the stem of grapevine and Cucurbita, are modified:
q.e: In grapevine and Cucurbita, the coiled tendrils used for climbing develop from axillary buds and are therefore stem tendrils.

q.q: Parallel venation, in which veins run parallel to each other within the lamina, is typically found in:
q.e: Parallel venation, where veins run parallel to one another within the lamina, is a characteristic feature of most monocotyledonous plants, e.g., banana, grasses.

q.q: A leaf whose lamina is entire, or if incised the incisions do not touch the midrib, is called a:
q.e: In a simple leaf, the lamina is entire, or if incised, the incisions do not reach the midrib; in a compound leaf the incisions reach the midrib, dividing the lamina into leaflets.

q.q: The main parts of a typical angiosperm leaf are the leaf base, petiole and:
q.e: A typical leaf consists of the leaf base, petiole and lamina (leaf blade), the green, expanded part of the leaf.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about compound leaves is/are correct?
(i) In a pinnately compound leaf, leaflets are arranged along a common axis (rachis)
(ii) In a palmately compound leaf, leaflets are attached at a common point
(iii) Neem shows a pinnately compound leaf
(iv) Silk cotton shows a palmately compound leaf
q.e: Pinnately compound leaves (e.g., Neem) have leaflets along a common rachis, while palmately compound leaves (e.g., Silk cotton) have leaflets attached at a common point — all four statements are correct.

q.q: In a racemose inflorescence, the opening of flowers from the base towards the apex is known as:
q.e: In racemose inflorescences, flowers open in acropetal succession — from the base towards the apex — since the main axis keeps growing and producing new flowers towards the top.

q.q: A spike differs from a raceme mainly in that its flowers are:
q.e: A spike is a racemose inflorescence bearing sessile (unstalked) flowers on the main axis, unlike a raceme where flowers have a pedicel.

q.q: In a capitulum (head) inflorescence, as seen in sunflower, the numerous small sessile flowers are arranged on a:
q.e: In a capitulum, the main axis is condensed to form a flat or slightly convex receptacle bearing numerous sessile flowers, giving the appearance of a single flower head, as in sunflower.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about cymose inflorescence is/are correct?
(i) The main axis terminates in a flower and is thus limited in growth
(ii) The oldest flower is at the top/centre while younger flowers develop laterally below it
(iii) It shows unlimited growth of the main axis
(iv) A uniparous cyme gives rise to only one lateral branch at a time
q.e: In cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower, so growth is limited; the oldest flower is at the top/centre, with younger ones arising laterally below it; a uniparous cyme produces only one lateral branch at a time.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a racemose inflorescence?
q.e: Mustard shows a racemose inflorescence (raceme), where the main axis continues to grow and bears flowers laterally in acropetal succession.

q.q: A flower that can be divided into two equal radial halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre is said to be:
q.e: A flower is actinomorphic (radially symmetrical) when it can be divided into two equal radial halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre, e.g., mustard, datura.

q.q: In epigynous flowers, the position of the ovary relative to the other floral whorls is:
o: Superior, with other whorls below it
Inferior, situated below the other floral whorls
q.e: In epigynous flowers, the ovary is inferior — situated below the other floral whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium), which appear to arise from the top of the ovary, as in guava and cucumber flowers.

q.q: The whorl of a flower that bears the pollen-producing organs is the:
q.e: The androecium is the male reproductive whorl of a flower, made up of stamens, each typically bearing an anther that produces pollen grains.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the calyx is/are correct?
(i) It is usually green and protects the flower in the bud stage
(ii) When the sepals are free, the calyx is termed polysepalous
(iii) The calyx is always the innermost whorl of a flower
(iv) In gamosepalous flowers, the sepals are united
q.e: The calyx, made up of sepals, is usually the outermost whorl, green, and protects the flower in bud; sepals may be free (polysepalous) or united (gamosepalous).

q.q: A fruit that develops from the ovary of a single flower with one or more carpels, as in mango, is termed a:
q.e: A fruit developing from the ovary of a single flower with one or more carpels is called a simple fruit, e.g., mango.

q.q: The wall of a fruit that develops from the wall of the ovary after fertilisation is called the:
q.e: The pericarp is the fruit wall that develops from the wall of the ovary after fertilisation; it may be dry or fleshy.

q.q: In a typical non-endospermous dicotyledonous seed, food reserves are mainly stored in the:
q.e: In non-endospermous dicot seeds (e.g., gram, pea), the endosperm is consumed during embryo development, and food is stored in the thick, fleshy cotyledons of the mature seed.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about seed structure is/are correct?
(i) The seed coat has two layers, testa (outer) and tegmen (inner)
(ii) The hilum is the scar on the seed coat where the seed was attached to the fruit
(iii) The micropyle is a small pore above the hilum through which water enters during germination
(iv) All mature seeds retain an endosperm
q.e: The seed coat has an outer testa and inner tegmen; the hilum marks the point of attachment to the fruit; the micropyle, above the hilum, allows water entry during germination. Not all mature seeds retain endosperm — in non-endospermous seeds it is consumed by the developing embryo.

q.q: The corolla of a typical Solanaceae flower is:
q.e: In Solanaceae, the corolla is gamopetalous (fused petals) with valvate aestivation, typically five-lobed and rotate, e.g., in Solanum (brinjal, tomato, potato).

q.q: The fruit typically found in members of family Solanaceae is a:
q.e: Solanaceae members typically bear a berry (e.g., tomato, brinjal) or a capsule (e.g., Datura) as fruit.

q.q: Members of family Solanaceae are economically important mainly because they provide:
o: Food, spice and medicinal plants (e.g., potato, chilli, ashwagandha)
q.e: Solanaceae is economically important, providing food (potato, tomato, brinjal), spice (chilli) and medicine (ashwagandha, belladonna).

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the androecium in a typical Solanaceae flower is/are correct?
(i) Stamens are usually five in number
(ii) Stamens are epipetalous (attached to the corolla tube)
(iii) The androecium is always polyandrous with numerous free stamens
(iv) Anthers are typically bilobed
q.e: In Solanaceae, the androecium typically has five stamens that are epipetalous (attached to the corolla) and have bilobed anthers, not numerous free stamens.

q.q: The waxy covering of the epidermis, generally absent in roots, is the:
q.e: The cuticle is the waxy layer covering aerial epidermis; roots lack it.

q.q: Guard cells in the stomatal apparatus of grasses are:
q.e: Grass guard cells are dumb-bell shaped.

q.q: A vascular bundle with cambium present, capable of secondary growth, is called:
q.e: Presence of cambium defines an open vascular bundle.

q.q: Match Column I (Term) with Column II (Meaning):
q.e: Trichome=multicellular stem hair; Root hair=unicellular outgrowth; Stomatal apparatus=aperture+guard+subsidiary cells.

q.q: Match Column I (Bundle type) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Open bundle has cambium (dicots); closed bundle has no cambium (monocots).

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Ground tissue system includes cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays
(ii) Vascular tissue system consists of xylem and phloem
(iii) Epidermal tissue system includes stomata and trichomes
q.e: All three statements correctly describe the respective tissue systems.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about vascular bundles is/are correct?
(i) Conjoint bundles have xylem and phloem on the same radius
(ii) Radial bundles are seen in roots
(iii) Open bundles lack cambium
q.e: Statements (i) and (ii) are correct; (iii) is wrong since open bundles HAVE cambium.

q.q: The single outer layer of the root producing root hairs is the:
q.e: The root's epidermis, called the epiblema, produces root hairs.

q.q: Casparian strips are composed of:
q.e: Casparian strips are waxy suberin deposits.

q.q: The number of xylem patches in a dicot root is typically:
q.e: Dicot roots show 2 to 4 xylem patches.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Pericycle initiates lateral roots; endodermis has Casparian strips; pith is small/inconspicuous.

q.q: Match Column I (Region) with Column II (Description):
q.e: Epiblema bears root hairs; cortex is thin-walled parenchyma with spaces; stele = pericycle+VB+pith.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the dicot root is/are correct?
(i) Xylem is exarch
(ii) Pith is large and prominent
(iii) Pericycle initiates lateral roots
q.e: (ii) is wrong — dicot root pith is small, not large; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about secondary growth in dicot roots is/are correct?
(i) It begins with cambium ring formation
(ii) The pericycle contributes to the cambium
(iii) Secondary growth never occurs in dicot roots
q.e: (iii) is wrong — secondary growth does occur in dicot roots; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: A vascular bundle with more than 6 xylem patches is:
q.e: More than 6 xylem patches defines polyarch.

q.q: Pith in a monocot root is:
q.e: Monocot root pith is large and well developed.

q.q: Secondary growth is absent in monocot roots because:
o: No vascular cambium forms between xylem and phloem
q.e: No cambium forms between xylem and phloem, so no secondary growth occurs.

q.q: Match Column I (Root type) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Dicot root: oligoarch, small pith; monocot root: polyarch, large pith.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Epiblema bears root hairs; pericycle never forms cambium in monocots; endodermis has Casparian strips.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about monocot roots is/are correct?
(i) Xylem is exarch
(ii) Pith is large
(iii) Secondary growth occurs regularly
q.e: (iii) is wrong — monocot roots never show secondary growth; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following is/are true for BOTH dicot and monocot roots?
(i) Radial vascular bundle
(ii) Exarch protoxylem
(iii) Same number of xylem patches
q.e: (i) and (ii) hold for both; (iii) is wrong, since xylem patch number differs (oligoarch vs polyarch).

q.q: In a T.S. of monocot root, the region containing more than six xylem patches around a large pith is the:
q.e: This region — pericycle, vascular bundle, and pith together — is the stele.

q.q: The hypodermis of a dicot stem is made of:
q.e: Dicot stem hypodermis is collenchymatous.

q.q: Vascular bundles in a dicot stem are arranged:
q.e: Dicot stem vascular bundles form a ring.

q.q: The endodermis of the dicot stem is also known as the:
q.e: It is rich in starch grains, hence called the starch sheath.

q.q: Match Column I (Region) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Hypodermis=collenchyma; pericycle=sclerenchyma patches; pith=large, central, parenchymatous.

q.q: Match Column I (Vascular bundle) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Dicot stem VB: conjoint, open, endarch; dicot root VB: radial, exarch.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the dicot stem is/are correct?
(i) Vascular bundles are conjoint and open
(ii) Xylem is endarch
(iii) Pith is absent
q.e: (iii) is wrong — dicot stem pith is present and well developed; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about medullary rays is/are correct?
(i) They lie between adjacent vascular bundles
(ii) They are made of radially placed parenchyma
(iii) They are vascular tissue
q.e: (iii) is wrong — medullary rays are ground (parenchymatous) tissue, not vascular tissue.

q.q: The hypodermis of the monocot stem is made of:
q.e: Monocot stem hypodermis is sclerenchymatous.

q.q: Vascular bundles in the monocot stem are:
q.e: Monocot stem vascular bundles are scattered.

q.q: Phloem parenchyma in the monocot stem's vascular bundle is:
q.e: Phloem parenchyma is absent in monocot stems.

q.q: Match Column I (Stem type) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Monocot stem: scattered VBs, no pith; dicot stem: ring of VBs, pith present.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Bundle sheath=sclerenchyma around VB; water cavity=where protoxylem broke down; ground tissue=undifferentiated cortex+pith.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the monocot stem is/are correct?
(i) Vascular bundles are closed
(ii) Pith is well developed
(iii) Hypodermis is sclerenchymatous
q.e: (ii) is wrong — monocot stems lack a distinguishable pith; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following is/are true for the monocot stem's vascular bundle?
(i) Conjoint
(ii) Endarch
(iii) Surrounded by a sclerenchymatous sheath
q.e: All three statements correctly describe the monocot stem's vascular bundle.

q.q: In a T.S. of monocot stem, the tissue filling the space around the scattered vascular bundles, between the hypodermis and the centre, is the:
q.e: This undifferentiated parenchymatous tissue is simply called ground tissue.

q.q: A dicot leaf, differentiated into palisade and spongy mesophyll, is termed:
q.e: Such a leaf is dorsiventral.

q.q: Palisade cells lie just below the:
q.e: Palisade cells lie below the adaxial (upper) epidermis.

q.q: The parenchyma layer surrounding the leaf's vascular bundle is the:
q.e: This layer is called the bundle sheath.

q.q: Match Column I (Tissue) with Column II (Description):
q.e: Palisade=elongated vertical cells; spongy=loosely arranged with air spaces; bundle sheath=surrounds vascular bundle.

q.q: Match Column I (Leaf type) with Column II (Venation):
q.e: Dicot leaf shows reticulate venation; monocot leaf shows parallel venation.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the dicot leaf is/are correct?
(i) Mesophyll is differentiated
(ii) More stomata occur on the abaxial surface
(iii) Venation is parallel
q.e: (iii) is wrong — dicot leaf venation is reticulate, not parallel; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about air cavities in the dicot leaf is/are correct?
(i) They occur between spongy mesophyll cells
(ii) They aid gas exchange
(iii) They occur within the vascular bundle
q.e: (iii) is wrong — air cavities occur in the mesophyll, not within the vascular bundle; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: A monocot leaf, similar on both surfaces, is termed:
q.e: Such a leaf is isobilateral.

q.q: Bulliform cells are located on the:
q.e: Bulliform cells occur on the adaxial epidermis, along the veins.

q.q: Stomatal distribution in the monocot leaf is:
q.e: Isobilateral leaves show roughly equal stomata on both surfaces.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Description):
q.e: Bulliform cell=large empty epidermal cell; bundle sheath=parenchyma around VB; mesophyll=undifferentiated chlorenchyma.

q.q: Match Column I (Cell state) with Column II (Leaf condition):
q.e: Turgid bulliform cells keep the leaf flat; flaccid bulliform cells cause it to curl.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the monocot leaf is/are correct?
(i) Mesophyll is undifferentiated
(ii) Venation is parallel
(iii) Stomata occur only on one surface
q.e: (iii) is wrong — stomata occur on both surfaces roughly equally; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about bulliform cells is/are correct?
(i) They are large and colourless
(ii) They help conserve water via leaf rolling
(iii) They are photosynthetic powerhouses
q.e: (iii) is wrong — bulliform cells are not chiefly photosynthetic; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: Radial vascular bundles are characteristic of:
q.e: Radial vascular bundles are found in roots.

q.q: Open vascular bundles, capable of secondary growth, occur in:
q.e: Open (cambium-containing) vascular bundles are a dicot feature.

q.q: Isobilateral leaves with undifferentiated mesophyll are typical of:
q.e: Isobilateral leaves, with undifferentiated mesophyll, are typical of monocots.

q.q: Match Column I (Root type) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Dicot root=oligoarch, small pith; monocot root=polyarch, large pith; dicot stem=ring of open VBs.

q.q: Match Column I (Leaf type) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Dicot leaf shows palisade+spongy mesophyll; monocot leaf shows bulliform cells.

q.q:
Which of the following statements comparing dicots and monocots is/are correct?
(i) Dicot stems show ring-arranged vascular bundles
(ii) Monocot stems show scattered vascular bundles
(iii) Both lack a pith
q.e: (iii) is wrong — dicot stems DO have a well-developed pith; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Exarch xylem occurs in both dicot and monocot roots
(ii) Endarch xylem occurs in both dicot and monocot stems
(iii) Bulliform cells occur in dicot leaves
q.e: (iii) is wrong — bulliform cells occur in monocot, not dicot, leaves; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: A T.S. shows scattered, closed, conjoint vascular bundles with a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath and no pith. This is best identified as a:
q.e: These are all classic monocot stem features.

q.q: The term 'cell' was first coined by:
q.e: Robert Hooke coined the term 'cell' in 1665.

q.q: The scientist who discovered the nucleus is:
q.e: Robert Brown discovered the nucleus.

q.q: The largest known single cell is:
q.e: The ostrich egg is the largest known single cell.

q.q: Match Column I (Scientist) with Column II (Contribution):
q.e: Hooke=coined 'cell'; Leeuwenhoek=first saw a live cell; Virchow=modified cell theory.

q.q: Match Column I (Cell/organelle type) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Cell theory was originally proposed by Schleiden and Schwann
(ii) Virchow added that all cells arise from pre-existing cells
(iii) Prokaryotic cells possess membrane-bound organelles
q.e: (iii) is wrong — prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about cell organelles is/are correct?
(i) Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound
(ii) Centrioles are present only in animal cells
(iii) All organelles in a eukaryotic cell are membrane-bound
q.e: (iii) is wrong — ribosomes and centrioles are non-membrane-bound; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: PPLO and Mycoplasma are examples of:
q.e: PPLO and Mycoplasma are prokaryotic organisms.

q.q: The infoldings of the plasma membrane in prokaryotes, aiding respiration and secretion, are called:
q.e: Mesosomes are plasma-membrane infoldings assisting respiration, secretion, wall formation and DNA distribution.

q.q: The subunits of a 70S prokaryotic ribosome are:
q.e: A 70S ribosome is made of 50S and 30S subunits.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Function):
q.e: Pili/fimbriae=attachment; flagella=locomotion; plasmid=antibiotic resistance.

q.q: Match Column I (Bacteria type) with Column II (Gram stain reaction):
q.e: Gram positive bacteria take up the stain; Gram negative bacteria do not.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles
(ii) Ribosomes are the only organelle found in prokaryotic cells
(iii) Mesosomes help in DNA replication and distribution
q.e: All three statements are correct — ribosomes are indeed the only (non-membrane-bound) organelle prokaryotes possess, alongside mesosomes' role in DNA replication/distribution.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about inclusion bodies is/are correct?
(i) They store reserve food material
(ii) They are bound by a membrane
(iii) Gas vacuoles are found in blue-green, purple and green bacteria
q.e: (ii) is wrong — inclusion bodies are NOT membrane-bound; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed by:
q.e: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model.

q.q: Water moves across the plasma membrane mainly by:
q.e: Water crosses membranes chiefly via osmosis.

q.q: The plant cell wall's primary component is:
q.e: Cellulose is the main component of the plant cell wall.

q.q: Match Column I (Transport type) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Passive transport needs no energy and moves along the gradient; active transport needs energy and moves against it.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Location/Role):
q.e: Middle lamella=cements cells (calcium pectate); plasmodesmata=connect cytoplasm; secondary wall=deposited later, inner side.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Integral proteins lie buried within the membrane
(ii) Peripheral proteins lie on the membrane's surface
(iii) Facilitated diffusion requires cellular energy
q.e: (iii) is wrong — facilitated diffusion is passive and needs no energy; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the cell wall is/are correct?
(i) It is present in plants and fungi
(ii) It is absent in animal cells
(iii) The algal cell wall may contain calcium carbonate
q.e: All three statements are correct — the cell wall occurs in plants/fungi, is absent in animals, and algal walls may contain minerals like CaCO3.

q.q: The endomembrane system does NOT include the:
q.e: The mitochondrion is excluded from the endomembrane system.

q.q: RER is chiefly associated with:
q.e: RER, with its ribosomes, is the site of protein synthesis.

q.q: The vacuolar membrane is called the:
q.e: The tonoplast is the vacuole's surrounding membrane.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Function):
q.e: SER=lipid synthesis; Golgi=packaging; lysosome=digestion.

q.q: Match Column I (Golgi face) with Column II (Description):
q.e: Cis=forming face; trans=maturing face.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Lysosomes are rich in hydrolytic enzymes
(ii) The endomembrane system includes mitochondria
(iii) The Golgi apparatus is made of stacked cisternae
q.e: (ii) is wrong — mitochondria are not part of the endomembrane system; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about the vacuole is/are correct?
(i) Its membrane is the tonoplast
(ii) The tonoplast cannot move ions against a gradient
(iii) Contractile vacuoles occur in Amoeba
q.e: (ii) is wrong — the tonoplast CAN pump ions against the gradient; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: Ribosomes were first observed by:
q.e: George Palade first observed ribosomes under the electron microscope.

q.q: The eukaryotic ribosome's Svedberg value is:
q.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S.

q.q: The infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane are called:
q.e: Cristae are infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Matrix=DNA/ribosomes; inner membrane=cristae; outer membrane=boundary.

q.q: Match Column I (Ribosome type) with Column II (S value):
q.e: Prokaryotic ribosome=70S; eukaryotic ribosome=80S.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Mitochondria have a double-membrane system
(ii) Ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles
(iii) The matrix contains a single circular DNA
q.e: (ii) is wrong — ribosomes are non-membrane-bound; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration
(ii) Mitochondria always divide together with the rest of the cell, never independently
(iii) Cristae increase the surface area of the inner membrane
q.e: (ii) is wrong — mitochondria can divide independently, by fission; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: Plastids bearing chlorophyll are called:
q.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are green.

q.q: A stack of thylakoids is called a:
q.e: A granum is a stack of thylakoids.

q.q: The chloroplast's own DNA and ribosomes are located in the:
q.e: The stroma contains the chloroplast's small circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.

q.q: Match Column I (Plastid) with Column II (Colour/Role):
q.e: Chloroplast=green/photosynthesis; chromoplast=non-green colour; leucoplast=colourless storage.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Description):
q.e: Stroma lamellae=connects grana; thylakoid=chlorophyll-bearing sac; lumen=space inside thylakoid.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) The chloroplast has a double membrane
(ii) The inner membrane is more permeable than the outer
(iii) Grana are stacks of thylakoids
q.e: (ii) is wrong — the inner membrane is LESS permeable; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about plastids is/are correct?
(i) Plastids occur in plant cells and euglenoids
(ii) Chromoplasts contain chlorophyll
(iii) Leucoplasts are colourless and used for storage
q.e: (ii) is wrong — chromoplasts do NOT contain chlorophyll, they contain other pigments; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: The functions of the cytoskeleton include all of the following EXCEPT:
q.e: Protein synthesis is not a cytoskeleton function; it provides support, motility and shape maintenance.

q.q: The number of peripheral microtubule pairs in an axoneme is:
q.e: The axoneme has 9 peripheral pairs plus 1 central pair (9+2 array).

q.q: Centrioles form the basal body of cilia/flagella and also help form the:
q.e: Centrioles help form the spindle fibre during cell division.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Cilia=shorter, oar-like; flagella=longer, fewer; basal body=origin structure.

q.q: Match Column I (Part of centriole) with Column II (Description):
q.e: Hub=central part; spoke=connects hub to triplets; peripheral fibril=a triplet of tubulin.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) The axoneme shows a 9+2 microtubule array
(ii) The centriole shows a 9+2 microtubule array
(iii) Both structures are made of tubulin protein
q.e: (ii) is wrong — the centriole is 9 triplets with NO central pair (9+0), not 9+2; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about microbodies is/are correct?
(i) They are membrane-bound
(ii) They are found only in animal cells
(iii) They contain enzymes
q.e: (ii) is wrong — microbodies occur in BOTH plant and animal cells; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: Mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells are notable because they lack a:
q.e: Both mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.

q.q: The nuclear matrix, consisting of the nucleolus and chromatin, is called the:
q.e: The nucleoplasm is the nuclear matrix, made of the nucleolus and chromatin.

q.q: A chromosome's primary constriction is called the:
q.e: The centromere is the chromosome's primary constriction.

q.q: Match Column I (Chromosome type) with Column II (Centromere position):
q.e: Metacentric=middle; acrocentric=close to end; telocentric=terminal point.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure) with Column II (Feature):
q.e: Nucleolus=rRNA synthesis; nuclear pore=RNA/protein transfer; perinuclear space=gap between nuclear membranes.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) The nucleolus is bound by a membrane
(ii) Chromatin condenses into chromosomes during cell division
(iii) Kinetochores lie on the sides of the centromere
q.e: (i) is wrong — the nucleolus is NOT membrane-bound; (ii) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements about chromosomes is/are correct?
(i) They contain DNA, histone and non-histone proteins
(ii) They never contain any RNA
(iii) Human DNA is distributed among 23 pairs of chromosomes
q.e: (ii) is wrong — chromosomes DO contain some RNA; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: The reagent used to fractionate living tissue during chemical analysis is:
q.e: TCA is used to grind tissue into a slurry for fractionation.

q.q: The molecular weight cut-off separating biomicromolecules from biomacromolecules is:
q.e: Under 1000 Da = micromolecule; over 1000 Da = macromolecule.

q.q: The percentage of water in the average cellular mass is approximately:
q.e: Water makes up 70-90% of a cell's mass, the most abundant component.

q.q: Match Column I (Fraction) with Column II (Contains):
q.e: Filtrate = acid-soluble = biomicromolecules; Retentate = acid-insoluble = biomacromolecules.

q.q: Match Column I (Element) with Column II (% in human body):
q.e: Carbon=18.5%, Oxygen=65.0%, Silicon=negligible in the human body.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Lipids are strictly macromolecules
(ii) Proteins are polymeric and acid-insoluble
(iii) Water is the most abundant chemical in a living cell
q.e: (i) is wrong — lipids are not strictly macromolecules (non-polymeric); (ii) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Elemental analysis of earth's crust and living tissue reveal completely different elements
(ii) The dry weight of tissue is obtained after evaporating all its water
(iii) Ash obtained after burning tissue contains inorganic compounds like Ca, Mg, S, P
q.e: (i) is wrong — the same elements are found in both, just in different proportions; (ii) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: In a schematic flow diagram of TCA fractionation (Tissue → Slurry → Filtration), the two end products shown are the filtrate and the:
q.e: Filtration of the TCA slurry yields a filtrate and a retentate (pellet).

q.q: The amino acid formed when R = CH3 is:
q.e: When R = CH3, the amino acid is alanine.

q.q: Palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid, has how many carbons (including the carboxyl carbon)?
q.e: Palmitic acid has 16 carbons including the carboxyl carbon.

q.q: The pH at which an amino acid exists purely as a zwitterion is called its:
q.e: This is defined as the isoelectric pH.

q.q: Match Column I (Amino acid category) with Column II (Example):
q.e: Acidic=glutamic acid; Basic=lysine; Aromatic=tyrosine.

q.q: Match Column I (Lipid-related compound) with Column II (Occurs in):
q.e: Sphingolipids=brain/nervous tissue; Steroids=hormones; Sterols=cholesterol/Vit D.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) An amino acid in acidic solution becomes positively charged
(ii) An amino acid in alkaline solution becomes positively charged
(iii) Fats have a lower melting point than oils
q.e: (ii) is wrong — alkaline solution makes it negatively charged; (iii) is wrong — fats have HIGHER melting points than oils; only (i) is correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Oleic, linoleic and linolenic acids are unsaturated fatty acids
(ii) Lecithin is a conjugated/phosphorylated lipid
(iii) Glycerol is a fatty acid
q.e: (iii) is wrong — glycerol is trihydroxy propane, not a fatty acid; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: Adenine and Guanine are together classified as:
q.e: Adenine and guanine are the two purine bases.

q.q: A nitrogenous base attached only to a sugar (no phosphate) is called a:
q.e: Base + sugar (no phosphate) = nucleoside.

q.q: Guanylic acid is formed by adding a phosphate group to:
q.e: Guanylic acid = guanosine + phosphate.

q.q: Match Column I (Base) with Column II (Nucleoside formed):
q.e: Adenine→adenosine; Thymine→thymidine; Cytosine→cytidine.

q.q: Match Column I (Category) with Column II (Members):
q.e: Purines=Adenine & Guanine; Pyrimidines=Thymine, Uracil & Cytosine.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) A nucleotide = nitrogenous base + sugar + phosphate
(ii) A nucleoside = nitrogenous base + phosphate (no sugar)
(iii) Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides
q.e: (ii) is wrong — a nucleoside is base + SUGAR (no phosphate); (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Purines have two fused rings
(ii) Pyrimidines have two fused rings
(iii) Adenylic acid is a nucleotide formed from adenine
q.e: (ii) is wrong — pyrimidines have ONE ring, not two; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: Cellulose is a homopolymer of:
q.e: Cellulose consists of beta-glucose units.

q.q: The glycosidic bond linking glucose units in starch is:
q.e: Starch's glucose units are joined by alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds.

q.q: Inulin is a storage homopolysaccharide made of:
q.e: Inulin is a polymer of fructose.

q.q: Match Column I (Polysaccharide) with Column II (Linkage):
q.e: Cellulose=beta-1,4; Starch=alpha-1,4.

q.q: Match Column I (Polysaccharide) with Column II (Role/Source):
q.e: Glycogen=animal storage; Chitin=arthropod exoskeleton/fungal wall; Pectin=plant cell wall.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Starch gives a blue colour with iodine
(ii) Cellulose gives a blue colour with iodine
(iii) Starch is branched and forms helical secondary structures
q.e: (ii) is wrong — cellulose (unbranched, no helix) does not give the iodine test; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Heteropolysaccharides are made of only one type of monomer
(ii) Chitin and pectin are heteropolysaccharides
(iii) Homopolysaccharides include cellulose, starch, glycogen and inulin
q.e: (i) is wrong — heteropolysaccharides have MORE than one type of (modified) sugar; (ii) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: Nucleic acids are polymers of:
q.e: Nucleic acids are polynucleotide chains.

q.q: The sugar found in DNA nucleotides is:
q.e: DNA contains 2'-deoxyribose.

q.q: Which base occurs in RNA but not in DNA?
q.e: Uracil is unique to RNA; DNA has thymine instead.

q.q: Match Column I (Nucleic acid) with Column II (Sugar):
q.e: DNA=deoxyribose; RNA=ribose.

q.q: Match Column I (Feature) with Column II (Nucleic acid):
q.e: DNA is double-stranded; RNA is single-stranded and contains uracil.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) DNA contains thymine
(ii) RNA contains thymine
(iii) Both DNA and RNA contain guanine
q.e: (ii) is wrong — RNA contains uracil, not thymine; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Successive nucleotides are linked by phosphodiester bonds
(ii) The base is attached to the sugar by a peptide bond
(iii) A nucleotide contains one base, one sugar and one (or more) phosphate group(s)
q.e: (ii) is wrong — the base-sugar bond is an N-glycosidic bond, not a peptide bond; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q: In a simplified diagram of a polynucleotide strand, the repeating backbone shown running along the length of the chain is made of alternating sugar and:
q.e: The backbone of a polynucleotide chain is an alternating sugar-phosphate chain.

q.q: Proteins are polymers of:
q.e: Proteins are built from amino acid units.

q.q: The most abundant protein in the human body is:
q.e: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body.

q.q: A protein becomes biologically active at the level of its:
q.e: The protein is biologically active once folded to its tertiary structure.

q.q: Match Column I (Protein) with Column II (Function):
q.e: Insulin=hormone; Trypsin=enzyme; Antibody=fights infection.

q.q: Match Column I (Structure level) with Column II (Description):
q.e: Primary=sequence; Secondary=helix/sheet; Tertiary=3-D active fold.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Proteins are heteropolymers
(ii) All proteins have a quaternary structure
(iii) Haemoglobin's quaternary structure has 2 alpha and 2 beta subunits
q.e: (ii) is wrong — quaternary structure only applies to multi-subunit proteins, not all; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Primary metabolites are directly involved in growth and reproduction
(ii) Amino acids and fatty acids are primary metabolites
(iii) Alkaloids like morphine are primary metabolites
q.e: (iii) is wrong — alkaloids are SECONDARY metabolites; (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: In a schematic diagram of the four levels of protein structure arranged left to right, the third stage shown (after the sequence, and after the helix/sheet folds) is the:
q.e: The order is primary → secondary → tertiary → quaternary; the third stage is tertiary structure.

q.q: Almost all enzymes are chemically composed of:
q.e: Nearly all enzymes are proteins.

q.q: The organic cofactor that binds tightly and permanently to the apoenzyme is the:
q.e: A prosthetic group is tightly/permanently bound, e.g. haem.

q.q: Carboxypeptidase requires which metal ion as a cofactor?
q.e: Carboxypeptidase requires Zn2+.

q.q: Match Column I (Cofactor type) with Column II (Example):
q.e: Prosthetic group=haem; Coenzyme=NAD/NADP; Metal ion=Zn2+.

q.q: Match Column I (Enzyme class) with Column II (Reaction type):
q.e: Hydrolases=hydrolysis; Isomerases=isomer interconversion; Ligases=joining compounds.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) A holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor
(ii) Ribozymes are protein enzymes
(iii) Enzymes from thermophilic organisms can remain active up to 80-90°C
q.e: (ii) is wrong — ribozymes are RNA, not protein; (i) and (iii) are correct.

q.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
(i) Oxidoreductases catalyse redox reactions
(ii) Transferases move a group between two substrates
(iii) Lyases catalyse hydrolysis of bonds
q.e: (iii) is wrong — lyases remove groups WITHOUT hydrolysis (that's hydrolases); (i) and (ii) are correct.

q.q: The energy needed to bring the substrate to its transition state is called:
q.e: This is the activation energy.

q.q: The substrate concentration at half of Vmax is called:
q.e: Km (Michaelis-Menten constant) is [S] at half Vmax.

q.q: Malonate competitively inhibits which enzyme?
